**Direct answer:** Both levels give each transaction a single snapshot. Repeatable Read still allows serialization anomalies, such as write skew. Serializable adds tracking of read/write dependencies and aborts a transaction when it would make the outcome non-serializable. At either level, the application must be ready to retry the whole transaction after a serialization failure (SQLSTATE `40001`). That is also advisable after a deadlock (`40P01`). Unique-violation and exclusion-violation errors need case-by-case judgment.

Caveat: the pages came back through a summarizing fetch tool, not as raw text. I haven't checked the quoted wording against the original pages.

**Claims and sources**

- Repeatable Read and Serializable both work from a snapshot taken at the start of the transaction's first non-transaction-control statement.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html

- Repeatable Read fails with "could not serialize access due to concurrent update" when the transaction tries to modify or lock a row that a concurrent transaction changed and committed after it began.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html

- Repeatable Read can produce results that match no serial execution. The manual's example is a read-only transaction that sees a batch's control record marked complete but not its detail records.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html

- Serializable prevents those anomalies. It can abort a transaction even when no row is written twice, with the error "could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions". The manual's example is two transactions that each sum one class and insert the result into the other.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html

- Serialization failures always carry SQLSTATE `40001`, and the message text can vary.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html

- Applications using either level must be prepared to retry transactions that fail with serialization errors. They should abort the current transaction and retry it from the beginning.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html

- The retry has to re-run the whole transaction, including the application logic that decides which SQL to run and which values to use. PostgreSQL doesn't retry automatically.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html

- Retry `40001` always. Retrying `40P01` (deadlock) is advisable.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html

- Retry `23505` (unique violation) and `23P01` (exclusion violation) only in some cases. They can be effectively serialization failures, for example when two sessions pick the same new primary key. They can also be persistent errors.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html

- A retry isn't guaranteed to succeed. Under heavy contention it may take many attempts, so use a retry limit and backoff. Where a prepared transaction is involved, progress may be impossible until it finishes.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html

- On Serializable, the application shouldn't rely on data read in a transaction that later aborts. It should retry until the transaction succeeds.
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html

**Not established:** The fetched Repeatable Read text didn't state `40001` for its error. I'm inferring that it is the same kind of failure, and the Serializable section and the serialization-failure handling page say all serialization failures use `40001`. I also couldn't confirm the summarizer's claim that read-only transactions never conflict at either level. For Serializable, the manual says read-only transactions can still be involved in or aborted by dependency conflicts. The `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` mode is the exception. It waits for a safe snapshot, so it doesn't fail this way.

Sources:
- https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html
- https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html
